messages.subject: Shiny HTML tags very slow
parts:
Hi All,

Trying to speed up a Shiny app I found that, too my surprise, the speed issues were caused by the simple HTML functions such as "em" "strong" and "br".

The following code illustrates this problem:

> timer(for(i in 1:100000) j=i)                                                  # Just test how long the looping takes.
Time difference of 0.03906202 secs
> timer(for(i in 1:100000) s =  paste0("<em>","test","</em>"))  # Create a simple tag
Time difference of 0.457031 secs
> timer(for(i in 1:100000) s =  em("test"))                                # Use the shiny function "em"
Time difference of 4.987287 secs                                           # 10 times slower. 
> 

This might not seem like an issue but when you are building a large table of HTML formatted values it can (and did) cause significant delays. 

David

(I'm working with Laz on a different email thread)

I'm investigating some other solutions for you but one thing you can do, if your tag objects do not carry HTML dependencies or write to <head> or make use of singleton() (and Laz's don't do any of that, I checked) you can wrap the large list of tag objects in htmltools::doRenderTags. Like so:

fluidPage(
  doRenderTags(
    lapply(1:10000, function(i) {
      selectInput(... # whatever
    })
  )
)

All this does is skip over the head, singleton, and dependency processing, and goes straight to the HTML rendering, returning the result as an HTML() object that can easily be included with the rest of the UI.

This will save about 50% of the rendering time in your case, Laz. I'm working on something else to make it much faster than that, will check back in in an hour or two hopefully.

My other idea was to make a doRenderTags implementation in C++. I was far enough along that I decided to keep going.

https://github.com/jcheng5/fasttags

Replace doRenderTags() with fastrender().

You probably don't have to do %dopar% now; if that still makes a difference then it might be the creation of the graph that's taking time now, not the rendering, as fasttags should render all of the tags in much less than one second.

With another day or two of effort I could probably get this to the point that it could fully replace renderTags, so htmltools rendering would just be fast without any more special tricks or caveats. I don't have that time to spare right at this moment but I've added it to our work backlog.

On Tuesday, August 30, 2016 at 4:01:15 AM UTC-4, David Lubinsky wrote:
Hi All,

Trying to speed up a Shiny app I found that, too my surprise, the speed issues were caused by the simple HTML functions such as "em" "strong" and "br".

The following code illustrates this problem:

> timer(for(i in 1:100000) j=i)                                                  # Just test how long the looping takes.
Time difference of 0.03906202 secs
> timer(for(i in 1:100000) s =  paste0("<em>","test","</em>"))  # Create a simple tag
Time difference of 0.457031 secs
> timer(for(i in 1:100000) s =  em("test"))                                # Use the shiny function "em"
Time difference of 4.987287 secs                                           # 10 times slower. 
> 

This might not seem like an issue but when you are building a large table of HTML formatted values it can (and did) cause significant delays. 

David

parts:
David,

That’s actually the approach we were going to take, if the Shiny tags were going to continue performing under par.

But with Joe’s recent addition (the fasttags package with fastrender() function), we can continue using Shiny’s tags without any degradation to performance.  I haven’t tested it against the raw text tags using paste0(), but it is EXTREMELY fast to process Shiny tags.  So fast, in fact, that it blew me away.  No need for paste0() with text for HTML now.

Give it a try.

~ Laz Peterson
Paravis, LLC

parts:
Besides generating the text, there are several other things a tag object *may* do.

The most important is attaching HTML dependencies. That's why you can add, say, a data table using DT::dataTableOutput and not worry about where the supporting JavaScript and CSS files come from.

There are also singleton() and tags$head() that are essentially an older attempt to support the same scenario that HTML dependencies now address.

In any case, if forming the HTML by hand is working for you, you probably don't need to worry. If the aforementioned were going to cause problems for you, you'd likely notice.

That said, it bums me out if the only reason you're avoiding tags is performance. I'll consider that another vote to make the fast C++ code path the default in a future release.
